# Diagnosing Rough Shifting in Manual Transmissions: The Case of the Infiniti G35

Symptoms like grinding gears or resistance during shifts often point to mechanical failure, but they can sometimes stem from hydraulic pressure issues that resolve themselves under specific load conditions. In the case of a 2005 Infiniti G35 experiencing difficulty shifting into second gear, particularly when the engine is at lower RPMs versus higher revs, the root cause likely lies in the clutch hydraulic system rather than worn synchronizers.

The user described a distinct pattern: grinding occurred at 3000 RPM but resolved spontaneously once the engine was revved to 4500 RPM and then allowed to idle down while engaging the gear. This behavior is classic for low fluid pressure or air in the clutch slave cylinder. When shifting into second, the driver typically releases the throttle slightly earlier than when shifting out of first. At lower RPMs, this reduced engine vacuum and hydraulic head pressure might not be sufficient to fully depress the clutch fork against spring tension if there is a restriction in the line or a weak master cylinder seal. By revving the engine higher, you generate greater hydraulic pressure in the system, forcing the slave cylinder piston far enough to disengage the clutch plate completely before the gear engagement happens.

When the mechanic at the dealership resolved this issue during an oil change without charging extra labor time, they likely performed a critical step often overlooked: bleeding the brake/clutch master cylinder reservoir or checking the fluid level and condition. Brake fluid is hygroscopic; it absorbs moisture from the air over time. As water content rises, the boiling point drops, leading to vapor bubbles under high pressure (aeration). These compressible bubbles act like a sponge in the line, preventing full clutch disengagement until enough pressure builds up to force them aside. Flushing out old fluid and refilling with fresh DOT 3 or DOT 4 likely restored consistent hydraulic pressure, eliminating the need for "revving" to compensate.

Another possibility is that the master cylinder reservoir was low on fluid. A common pitfall in diagnosing this issue is assuming the pedal feels spongy due to a leak when it is actually just dry friction. If the reservoir dips below the minimum line, air can be drawn into the system during normal operation. Topping off the fluid and ensuring the cap seal is intact would have been a routine part of an oil change service at a dealership.

If you encounter similar symptoms in your own vehicle, start by checking the clutch fluid level and the condition of the lines for leaks before assuming the transmission internals are shot. While synchronizer wear can cause grinding under load, it rarely disappears completely just because you changed the oil or adjusted hydraulic pressure. The fact that the issue vanished after a standard service suggests a maintenance-related fix rather than a catastrophic mechanical failure requiring a rebuild.

In this case, increasing one variable (RPM) masked the underlying pressure deficit. The permanent solution addressed the system's baseline health.
